events.content:
Like many a nerd, I have a certain fascination with locks. This originates in reading the memoir Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman as a teenager, in which Richard Feynman recounts picking locks and cracking combinations while at his day job working on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos. I currently have a couple of locksport pick sets and training locks that I purchased at hacker conferences over the years (although I’m still terrible at it), and I delight in the YouTube exploits of folks like the LockPickingLawyer.
All of which left me wondering if I could try building an interesting lock. One dodge that lockmakers have long used to challenge would-be plunderers is to conceal the existence of the lock itself. A modern variant of this is the magnetic lock, where a magnet is held or slid against an innocuous portion of a door or box, releasing a catch. The problem with this is that, once you guess the location of the lock, any strong magnet will open it.
So I started thinking about embedding an RFID reader under the surface and resigning myself to keeping track of yet another access card. But then I stumbled across something much more interesting: SparkFun’s US $100 magnetic imaging tile. I realized I could use this to build a magnetic lock that opens with a programmable secret gesture.
 I used a few discrete components to drive the servo motor and put the lock into program mode [top], controlled by a Teensy 4.1 microcontroller [middle]. An array of Hall-effect sensors detect magnetic fields [bottom].James Provost
The magnetic imaging tile is a small-run SparkFun board based on the work of Peter Jansen. It features an 8-by-8 grid of Hall-effect sensors, and uses an SPI interface to talk to the microcontroller of your choice. These sensors can detect both the magnitude and polarity of a magnetic field, and the board can report its measurements hundreds to thousands of times per second, depending on how much processing power your microcontroller has available. This is easily fast enough to capture the motion of a magnet being moved by hand across the board’s sensor area—my secret gesture.
An interesting thing about using magnetic fields is that if I was in extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting, something I couldn’t do with an RFID reader. The copper sheet would act as a Faraday cage, blocking any RFID signal, along with any other electromagnetic fields an attacker with an EMF meter might use to locate the lock.
Choosing the Brains of the BoxI chose a Teensy 4.1 as my microcontroller. I like the Teensy because it offers loads of input/output, a 600-megahertz processor, a megabyte of RAM, and a built-in SD card, all in a slim package with an equally slim $32 price tag.
Wiring the Teensy to the magnetic-imaging tile was trivial, only complicated by the fact that one side of the board has a silk-screen error that misidentifies the SPI connections (SparkFun says this will be fixed in future runs of the board).
In extreme paranoia mode, I could shield the entire lock behind copper sheeting.
To create the gesture-recognition software, I once again turned to vibe coding. If you read my Hands On piece in the April 2026 issue of IEEE Spectrum on creating a teletext suite for ham radio, you’ll know I’ve been grappling with how vibe coding should be used in DIY projects, if at all. So this time, instead of letting Claude write all the software, I confined it to writing just two support libraries, which you can find in our online repository at https://github.com/IEEESpectrumHandsOn.
One library is in charge of recording a lock gesture and saving it to the Teensy’s nonvolatile storage. The other library monitors the tile and reports whether or not a newly detected gesture passes a selectable threshold to be considered a match.

Appearing on the Colin and Samir podcast to talk about the launch of widescreen and long-form video for Instagram, Mosseri said he thinks there's a trend of "more anxiety and more frustration and more anger about AI," particularly in creative industries:

events.title: 欧央行行长拉加德：基础通胀稳定，工资压力温和，融资条件已经收紧，不预设利率路径
events.summary:
当地时间周四，欧洲央行行长克里斯蒂娜·拉加德（Christine Lagarde）在10月货币政策新闻发布会上宣布，管理委员会一致决定维持三大关键利率不变。在经历了中东地缘冲突引发的能源市场动荡后，欧洲央行选择在高度不确定的宏观环境下“按兵不动”。

拉加德在整场发布会中试图将市场的注意力集中在基础通胀的稳定上，并明确表示央行正在采用一种基于数据的观望策略。

拉加德在开场声明中直言不讳地指出了当前的宏观矛盾：“能源价格继续上涨，对通胀前景构成上行风险，对增长前景构成下行风险。”

淡化“二轮效应”：基础通胀稳定，工资压力温和
市场高度关注近期能源暴涨是否会引发更广泛的通胀失控。数据显示，欧元区通胀从8月的3.2%显著升至9月的3.8%，其中能源价格通胀从14.3%飙升至18.9%。剔除能源的核心通胀也从2.1%小幅攀升至2.3%。

然而，拉加德大量引用了底层数据来安抚市场对通胀全面扩散的担忧。她明确指出：

“尽管能源冲击的全面影响仍在显现，但迄今为止基础通胀大体稳定，工资在此阶段也未显示出实质性反应。”

针对市场最为担忧的“工资-通胀”螺旋上升（即二轮效应），拉加德给出了关键的数据支撑：

“工资压力仍然温和。第二季度雇员人均薪酬增长3.3%，低于第一季度的3.6%，而生产率上升有助于抑制单位劳动力成本增长。”

这一表态有力地打消了市场对央行因短期通胀反弹而被迫激进加息的
events.content:
当地时间周四，欧洲央行行长克里斯蒂娜·拉加德（Christine Lagarde）在10月货币政策新闻发布会上宣布，管理委员会一致决定维持三大关键利率不变。在经历了中东地缘冲突引发的能源市场动荡后，欧洲央行选择在高度不确定的宏观环境下“按兵不动”。

拉加德在整场发布会中试图将市场的注意力集中在基础通胀的稳定上，并明确表示央行正在采用一种基于数据的观望策略。

拉加德在开场声明中直言不讳地指出了当前的宏观矛盾：“能源价格继续上涨，对通胀前景构成上行风险，对增长前景构成下行风险。”

淡化“二轮效应”：基础通胀稳定，工资压力温和
市场高度关注近期能源暴涨是否会引发更广泛的通胀失控。数据显示，欧元区通胀从8月的3.2%显著升至9月的3.8%，其中能源价格通胀从14.3%飙升至18.9%。剔除能源的核心通胀也从2.1%小幅攀升至2.3%。

然而，拉加德大量引用了底层数据来安抚市场对通胀全面扩散的担忧。她明确指出：

“尽管能源冲击的全面影响仍在显现，但迄今为止基础通胀大体稳定，工资在此阶段也未显示出实质性反应。”

针对市场最为担忧的“工资-通胀”螺旋上升（即二轮效应），拉加德给出了关键的数据支撑：

“工资压力仍然温和。第二季度雇员人均薪酬增长3.3%，低于第一季度的3.6%，而生产率上升有助于抑制单位劳动力成本增长。”

这一表态有力地打消了市场对央行因短期通胀反弹而被迫激进加息的恐慌。

融资条件显著收紧，增长前景偏下行，通胀前景偏上行
在经济增长方面，欧洲央行展现出了谨慎的态度。虽然最新数据表明欧元区经济在第三季度继续扩张，且服务业、制造业和AI相关的商业投资仍在提供支撑，但高利率的滞后效应正在显现。

拉加德在发布会上强调了金融环境的变化：

“自我们上次会议以来，融资条件已经收紧，这可能拖累通胀和增长。” 

她用具体数据描绘了信贷市场的寒意：

“企业市场债务成本从7月的4.0%升至8月的4.1%，由于利率上升，抵押贷款需求大幅下降。”

关于未来的风险分布，拉加德给出了明确的指引：

“增长前景的风险偏向下行，通胀前景的风险偏向上行。”

她特别提到了中东冲突以及俄罗斯对乌克兰的战争等地缘政治因素，警告称：

“能源供应持续中断可能导致能源价格进一步上涨，这将拖累实际收入、支出和投资。”

拒绝预设路径，“逐次会议”决定未来
对于投资者最关心的未来利率路径和增长的可持续性想象空间，拉加德拒绝给出确定性的前瞻指引，而是将主动权交给了未来的经济数据。

“我们仍处于有利位置，能够应对当前高度不确定性。”拉加德重申了央行的政策框架：

“我们将采用依赖数据、逐次会议的方式来确定适当的货币政策立场，我们不预先承诺特定的利率路径。”

她补充道，未来的利率决策将基于三大支柱：“对通胀前景及其周围风险的评估”、“基础通胀动态”以及“货币政策传导力度”。

在发布会的最后，拉加德向市场传达了央行的底线：

“我们准备在职责范围内调整所有工具，以确保通胀可持续地稳定在我们的中期目标，并维护货币政策传导的顺畅运行。”

拉加德新闻发布会原文翻译：

下午好。我和副行长欢迎各位参加我们的新闻发布会。

管理委员会今天决定维持欧洲央行三大关键利率不变。

能源价格继续上涨，对通胀前景构成上行风险，对增长前景构成下行风险。尽管能源冲击的全面影响仍在显现，但迄今为止基础通胀大体稳定，工资在此阶段也未显示出实质性反应。

能源冲击的幅度和持续时间增加，以及对间接效应和二轮效应的影响，可能推高通胀并压低增长。

自我们上次会议以来，融资条件已经收紧，这可能拖累通胀和增长。我们致力于制定货币政策，以确保通胀在中期稳定在2%的目标。

我们仍处于有利位置，能够应对当前高度不确定性。我们将采用依赖数据、逐次会议的方式来确定适当的货币政策立场。特别是，我们的利率决策将基于我们对通胀前景及其周围风险的评估，并结合即将公布的经济和金融数据、基础通胀动态以及货币政策传导力度。我们不预先承诺特定的利率路径。

今天作出的决定已在我们网站发布的新闻稿中列明。

我现在将更详细地阐述我们如何看待经济和通胀的发展，然后解释我们对金融和货币条件的评估。

经济活动
最新数据表明，欧元区经济在第三季度继续扩张。服务业在中东冲突初期走弱后已经复苏。制造业、数字服务和出口正受益于人工智能相关商业投资。政府在基础设施和国防方面的支出也在支撑经济活动。这些因素应继续支撑近期增长。与此同时，能源价格重新上涨打击了消费者信心，融资成本上升可能拖累增长。

8月失业率仍为6.4%。就业和劳动力增长仍然低迷，而生产率已逐步回升。

中期内，能源价格逐步下降和劳动力市场稳健所推动的信心和实际收入复苏，应会提振国内需求。人工智能相关活动投资以及政府在基础设施和国防方面的支出也应继续支持增长。随着外需增强，出口增长应会加快。

提高潜在增长需要结构性改革，并且必须以健全的公共财政为支撑。财政可持续性是更广泛经济稳定的关键锚。对能源冲击的财政应对应是临时性、有针对性和量身定制的。简化并协调欧盟单一市场规则、加快能源转型以及完成储蓄与投资联盟，是使我们的经济更有活力和韧性的关键基石。随着数字欧元法律框架的达成进程进入最后阶段，我们重申尽快就单一货币一揽子方案达成协议的重要性。

通胀
通胀从8月的3.2%升至9月的3.8%。能源价格通胀显著上升，从8月的14.3%升至18.9%。柴油和汽油价格在9月创下新高，部分反映了炼油利润率上升。剔除能源的通胀从8月的2.1%升至9月的2.3%。食品价格通胀从1.1%升至1.3%。服务通胀从8月的3.0%升至9月的3.2%，而商品通胀从1.2%降至1.1%。

基础通胀指标大体稳定，但定价链早期阶段显示出上行压力。工资压力仍然温和。第二季度雇员人均薪酬增长3.3%，低于第一季度的3.6%，而生产率上升有助于抑制单位劳动力成本增长。我们的前瞻性工资追踪指标显示，2026年剩余月份协商工资增长将在2.5%至2.8%之间波动，并在2027年前三个季度平均为2.6%。较短期限的通胀预期已经上升，但多数长期通胀预期指标仍约为2%，支持中期通胀稳定在目标附近。

能源价格涨幅已超过欧洲央行工作人员9月预测中的基线路径。这可能在近期进一步推高通胀，并使整体通胀在未来几个季度远高于目标。此后，能源通胀下降以及更高利率的影响，应支持通胀回归目标。

风险评估
增长前景的风险偏向下行。这尤其源于中东冲突以及俄罗斯对乌克兰不正当战争的最新事态发展。能源供应持续中断可能导致能源价格进一步上涨，且上涨时间比目前预期更长。这将拖累实际收入、支出和投资。全球金融市场情绪恶化或全球债券市场溢出效应加剧，可能收紧融资条件，从而抑制需求。财政不确定性也可能进一步收紧融资条件并削弱信心，从而降低消费和投资。主要经济体之间贸易紧张局势重燃，可能进一步扰乱供应链、减少出口并削弱消费和投资。相反，如果经济和能源市场比预期更快地适应持续冲突造成的扰动，或者这些冲突得到可持续解决，增长可能高于预期。此外，欧元区企业采用新技术、政府在基础设施和国防方面的支出，以及提高生产率和完成欧盟单一市场的改革，可能比预期更多地推动增长。

通胀前景的风险偏向上行。这尤其源于中东冲突以及俄罗斯对乌克兰不正当战争的最新事态发展。能源冲击可能进一步加剧，其对其他价格和工资的影响可能比目前预期更强。尤其是天然气价格，如果供应进一步中断，或者异常寒冷的冬季恰逢低库存水平，可能上涨。能源价格保持高位的时间越长，就越可能通过间接效应和二轮效应推高更广泛的通胀。贸易紧张局势重燃可能导致全球供应链更加碎片化，削减关键原材料供应，并加剧欧元区经济的产能约束。极端天气事件——可能因“厄尔尼诺”条件加剧而强化——以及更广泛的气候和自然危机持续发展，可能比预期更多地推高食品价格。相反，如果持续的地缘政治冲突得到可持续解决，或者能源价格上涨带来的间接效应或二轮效应比预期更不明显，通胀可能低于预期。更加波动且风险厌恶的金融市场，加上更高的长期利率，可能拖累需求，从而降低通胀。

金融和货币条件
自我们上次会议以来，金融条件已经收紧。利率普遍上升，而股价下跌。

企业市场债务成本从7月的4.0%升至8月的4.1%，而银行对企业贷款利率仍为3.8%。银行对企业贷款增长从7月的4.4%放缓至8月和9月的年率4.2%，而公司债券发行在9月以年率4.2%增长，高于8月的3.8%和7月的3.5%。正如我们最新银行贷款调查所报告，第三季度对企业贷款的信贷标准收紧，银行称担心其客户面临的经济风险。尽管库存和营运资金的融资需求上升，企业贷款需求仍下降，尤其反映了更高利率的影响。

抵押贷款利率从7月的3.5%升至8月的3.6%，而抵押贷款增长在9月小幅降至3.0%。第三季度抵押贷款信贷标准保持不变，而由于利率上升，抵押贷款需求大幅下降。

结论
管理委员会今天决定维持欧洲央行三大关键利率不变。我们致力于制定货币政策，以确保通胀在中期稳定在2%的目标。我们将采用依赖数据、逐次会议的方式来确定适当的货币政策立场。我们的利率决策将基于我们对通胀前景及其周围风险的评估，并结合即将公布的经济和金融数据、基础通胀动态以及货币政策传导力度。我们不预先承诺特定的利率路径。

无论如何，我们准备在职责范围内调整所有工具，以确保通胀可持续地稳定在我们的中期目标，并维护货币政策传导的顺畅运行。

events.content:
How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World

Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models.

Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world.

I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle.

By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens").

Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request.

Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat.

This is continuous deployment turned up to 11:

A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...]

We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work.

My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well.

Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working:

Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off.

These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do.

Don’t let us tell you where you can or cannot put your Varmblixt. But it’s meant to sit on a table or be mounted on a wall (it can hang from a drilled-in screw, nothing fancy). At just 180 lumens, it isn’t particularly bright, so it’s better suited for use as a bedside lamp or for mood lighting than being tasked to illuminate a room. The newer model lets you cycle through 12 preset colors, including shades of pink, blue, green, and white, as opposed to just orange with the predecessor. The included wireless remote lets you switch between colors, adjust the brightness, and turn the lamp on or off without needing an app or a separate hub (there’s a power button on the lamp itself) . You can also use the remote to control other compatible Ikea lights.

For those who want to embed the Varmblixt into their smart home setup, the lamp supports Matter, allowing it to work with compatible smart home platforms including Apple Home, Google Home, and Amazon Alexa. In addition to letting you control the lights with your voice, this gives you access to hundreds more colors, lets you set lighting schedules and sleep or wake-up routines, and allows you to connect the lamp with motion sensors and other smart lights you may have. You can unlock those features with Ikea’s Dirigera hub, as well, which also offers a feature through its Home Smart app that gradually adjusts the shade of white throughout the day akin to natural daylight.

Read our Ikea Varmblixt review.

events.content:
The US power sector could release 42 percent more planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution by 2030 than it did in 2025 as it builds out more fossil fuel infrastructure to meet data center electricity demand, according to a new analysis by the Sierra Club. That would essentially wipe out 15 years of greenhouse gas reductions.

CO2 emissions from electricity generation would increase by 618 million tons by the end of the decade if planned AI projects are constructed. That's roughly equivalent to carbon pollution from the electricity use of 128,788,523 homes in a year.

events.title: The Download: AI agent tracking and climate feedback loops
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Opinion: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time —Madhulika Srikumar and Claire Leibowicz from the Partnership on AI, a nonprofit advancing best practices in AI governance. AI…
events.content:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Opinion: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time

—Madhulika Srikumar and Claire Leibowicz from the Partnership on AI, a nonprofit advancing best practices in AI governance.

AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, from hacking websites to accessing private government files. In many cases, they’ve eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them. 

As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability.

In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. Because right now, we’re effectively flying blind when deploying these tools. 

Here’s what needs to change.

Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot

Climate change itself increasingly fuels climate change. Rising greenhouse gas concentrations are driving up global temperatures, creating dangerous feedback loops that aren’t fully represented in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming. Now, a growing number of observations and studies are indicating how powerful these cascading effects could be. By extension, they’re also showing how much faster the planet may warm this century.

Read more about the dangerous feedback loops accelerating global warming.

—James Temple

This article is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.

Are we there yet? Solid-state batteries 

Lithium-ion batteries power everything from personal electronics to grid-scale energy storage, but their liquid electrolytes have drawbacks, not least a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer.

The technology promises faster charging, longer life, greater energy density and improved safety, and a new generation of companies aims to bring it to market. If their bets pan out, the tech could ease the shift away from fossil fuels.

Find out how close solid-state batteries are to delivering on their promise.

—Alexander C. Kaufman

This story is part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Hackers exposed 41,000 Homeland Security workers
Including undercover ICE agents. (Wired $)
+ Much of the data relates to Customs and Border Protection. (TechCrunch)
+ It also linked the agencies to specific surveillance tools. (Reuters $)
+ Big Tech is pushing back against ICE’s demands for user data. (WSJ $)
+ Activists want ChatGPT users to quit over ICE ties. (MIT Technology Review)

2 Putin says Russia is coordinating with “genius” Musk on satellites
He said the cooperation maintains order in orbit. (Bloomberg $)
+ Russia is developing its own version of Starlink. (Guardian)
+ Moscow added Apple and Microsoft to a surveillance registry. (Quartz)
+ Here’s all the stuff we’ve put up in space. (MIT Technology Review)

3 Apple just announced its first-ever MacBook with a touchscreen
It joins a blitz of product launches under new CEO John Ternus. (CNN)
+ Steve Jobs and Tim Cook had both dismissed the idea. (NYT $)
+ Executives say touchscreen advances mean it’s now worthwhile. (Wired $)

4 Bloomberg and trading firms are paying to get Trump’s posts faster
They’ve signed up for Truth Social’s pay-for-access plan. (Reuters $)

events.title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
events.summary: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem…
events.content:
This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them. 

AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility. 

Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes. That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today.

As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability: the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely.

Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important.

With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions. 

The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken.

Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer app

events.title: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
events.summary: Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals. Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of…
events.content:
Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century.

A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs, and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding. 

None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries.

A separate analysis published in One Earth in March, which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds.

Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group. 

At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project, through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds.

But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue. 

So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story). In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetl

events.title: Infini-AI-Lab Releases Hermit, an Open-Source Harness Adapter Framework for AI Agents
events.summary:
Infini-AI-Lab released Hermit, an Apache-2.0 harness adapter framework that trains an external layer of instructions, skills, memory and tools from task feedback, leaving the agent’s model and harness unchanged.

The post Infini-AI-Lab Releases Hermit, an Open-Source Harness Adapter Framework for AI Agents appeared first on MarkTechPost.
events.content:
Infini-AI-Lab has released Hermit, an open-source harness adapter framework for AI agents. Hermit is a framework from Infini-AI-Lab that trains an external ‘harness adapter’ while the agent’s model and harness stay frozen. The first release, v0.1.0, shipped on October 25, 2026. CMU postdoc Haizhong Zheng announced it on X on October 27. For developers, the pitch is simple: adapt Codex or Claude Code agents to new tasks without fine-tuning or forking the harness. TL;DR Footprint: A Python framework. No parameters of its own. Apache-2.0, pip install hermit-harness. Runs on: The offline Quick Start needs no GPU, model account or dataset. Real runs use any API backend or a local vLLM, SGLang or Ollama server. Performance: Reported gains over no-adapter baselines on OfficeQA, CL-Bench and ServeLearnBench, all with GLM 5.3 Flash. Best: MWM adapter hits 0.795 accuracy on CL-Bench database exploration, vs 0.580 for the in-context baseline. Worst: The prompt-only adapter scores 0.470 on the same venue, below that 0.580 baseline. Bottom line: Best: one training loop for 5 harness evolution methods. Worst: most results are single runs, self-reported. What is a harness adapter? A harness adapter is a trainable external harness. It works like a plugin with training support built in. A model adapter, such as LoRA, adapts a model. A harness adapter adapts an existing agent instead. The adapter can hold instructions, skills, memory, tools, executable code and agent coordination logic. It can even be a whole repository. Its specification says which parts are learnable and how updates get checked. The base model and harness never change. The team gives 3 reasons for this design. Many harnesses are closed-source. Editing open ones can break carefully tuned component interactions. And a learned adapter can move between compatible models and harnesses. How does Hermit train an adapter? Hermit uses an RL-style training loop. A Trainer runs a batch of tasks through the acting agent with the current adapter. A judge scores the outputs. An Evolver reads the trajectories and feedback, then proposes a new adapter. The Trainer checks it against the template and commits it as the next version. Every adapter version lives in a git tree. You can inspect, roll back or ship any version. Learner programs can run sandboxed, which requires Linux with bubblewrap. Five evolution methods ship today: GEPA, SkillOpt, MetaWorld Model (MWM), Harness² and Continual Harness. ACE and ReHarness are listed as coming soon. You can also write your own Evolver. Play Adapter version V0

Built-in Evolvers: GEPA, SkillOpt, MetaWorld Model (MWM), Harness², Continual Harness. ACE and ReHarness are listed as coming soon.

Self-reported results, all with GLM 5.3 Flash as the acting model. Pick a benchmark.

Train once, then deploy the adapter into an agent workspace or export it as a native plugin.

$ pip install hermit-harness $ hermit train --config run.yaml $ hermit eval --config run.yaml --adapter final $ hermit deploy --adapter DIR --workspace WS --host codex $ hermit convert --adapter DIR --output OUT --target claude-code # other convert targets: codex, pi, hermes

events.title: Block Unveils Dessa, a Full-Duplex Speech Model Trained Only on Speech
events.summary:
Block’s AI lab released Dessa, a full-duplex speech-to-speech model trained only on human conversation audio. It runs locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max, but Block has published no size, benchmarks or weights.

The post Block Unveils Dessa, a Full-Duplex Speech Model Trained Only on Speech appeared first on MarkTechPost.
events.content:
Block’s AI research lab has released Dessa, a full-duplex speech model trained only on human conversation. Block announced it on October 23, 2026 as a research preview. Dessa is a speech-to-speech model from Block that listens and talks at the same time. Block says it used no text and no pretrained models. That is a different design from the text-first stacks behind most voice agents today.

TL;DR

Runs on: A MacBook Pro M4 Max or better, locally, faster than real time. 

Performance: Demo-only so far. Live recordings show backchannels, mid-sentence laughs and natural interruptions.

Best: Trained on 1 NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 rack (72 GPUs). Moshi used 1,016 H100 GPUs.

Worst: 0 published benchmark scores. No weights, paper, API or price.

What is Block’s Dessa?

Dessa is a true speech-to-speech model: audio in, audio out. According to Block’s project page, everything it knows came from human speech.

It is full-duplex, so it listens while it talks. Block says it learned from real conversation when to cut in. It also learned when to backchannel with short cues like “yeah” or “got it”.

Block’s demo clips show Dessa laughing mid-sentence and getting louder when asked to speak up. One clip shows it talking with OpenAI’s GPT-Live-1. Block says nobody steered any clip.

How does speech-only training work?

Most voice systems chain 3 parts: speech recognition, a text model, then speech synthesis. Block team argues that chain throws away emotion, sarcasm, laughter and sighs. Dessa hears and produces those signals directly.

Block has not published the architecture. Here is what it has disclosed:

Training data: human conversation audio only. No text and no pretrained models.

Compute: 1 NVIDIA GB200 NVL72, which links 72 Blackwell GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs.

Data efficiency: Block says Dessa learned language from hundreds of times fewer words than LLMs need.

Inference: faster than real time, on a MacBook Pro M4 Max or better.

The lab also explains why this is hard. Speech never repeats exactly. A spoken word takes thousands of times more bytes than the same word in text.

Kyutai’s Moshi, the best-known open full-duplex model, takes another route. Moshi starts from a text language model backbone and predicts time-aligned text tokens before audio tokens. Its model card lists 7 million hours of pretraining audio and 1,016 H100 GPUs.

 

How does Dessa compare with Moshi, PersonaPlex and GPT-Live-1?

FeatureDessa (Block)Moshi (Kyutai)PersonaPlex-7B-v1 (NVIDIA)GPT-Live-1 (OpenAI)Starting pointSpeech only, no text, no pretrained modelHelium text LM backbone plus audioFine-tuned from Moshi (Moshiko) weightsNot disclosed; delegates reasoning to a backend agentParametersNot disclosed8B (Hugging Face listing)7B (model card)Not disclosedTraining compute1 GB200 NVL72 (72 GPUs)1,016 H100 GPUsNot disclosedNot disclosedTraining audioNot disclosed7M h unsupervised, 2,000 h Fisher, 20,000 h syntheticFisher English, under 10,000 hNot disclosedLatencyNot disclosed (“faster than real time”)200 ms in practice, 160 ms theoretical0.170 s turn-taking, 0.240 s interruption (FullDuplexBench)Not disclosed on model pageWeights and licenseNot releasedOpen, CC-BY 4.0Open, NVIDIA Open Model LicenseClosedRuns onMacBook Pro M4 Max or betterGPU; MLX, Candle and PyTorch checkpointsNVIDIA A100 / H100, LinuxOpenAI cloudAccess and priceResearch preview, waitlistFree downloadFree download (gated)API, $0.05 per minute voice layer

Key Takeaways

Dessa is full-duplex and speech-to-speech, trained only on human conversation audio.

Block trained it on 1 GB200 NVL72 rack; Moshi used 1,016 H100s.

It runs locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max, faster than real time.

Block published 0 benchmarks, no parameter count and no weights.

Access is a waitlist.

Check out the Dessa project page. Compare it with the Moshi paper, the PersonaPlex model card and the GPT-Live-1 docs. Also,feel free to follow us onTwitterand don’t

events.title: AssemblyAI Ships AssemblyAI-TTS-1: A $15 per 1M Character Text-to-Speech API for Voice Agents
events.summary:
AssemblyAI has released AssemblyAI-TTS-1, its first text-to-speech model for voice agents. It costs $15 per 1M characters, offers unlimited concurrency without a contract, and supports 6 languages at launch.

The post AssemblyAI Ships AssemblyAI-TTS-1: A $15 per 1M Character Text-to-Speech API for Voice Agents appeared first on MarkTechPost.
events.content: AssemblyAI has released AssemblyAI-TTS-1, its first text-to-speech model, now generally available. The AssemblyAI-TTS-1 text-to-speech API targets voice agents running on live phone calls. In that setting, latency and pronunciation decide whether a caller stays on the line. Pricing is $15 per 1M characters, with no annual contract and no concurrency tier to buy. For developers already using AssemblyAI speech-to-text, it closes the voice loop with one vendor. TL;DR Size: It is a hosted API model. Runs on: AssemblyAI’s cloud only, in the US (us-east-1) or EU (eu-north-1). No open weights or on-prem option. Any client with HTTP or WebSocket works. Performance: Ties ElevenLabs v4 on entity accuracy in AssemblyAI’s tests, at under 1/5 of its price. Best: 47 ms median time to first byte across 6 models in AssemblyAI’s API test (self-reported). Worst: 159 ms median streaming latency on Cekura’s independent benchmark, 8th of 19 timed models. Bottom line: Best: $15 per 1M characters with unlimited concurrency. Worst: no SSML, speed control, pronunciation dictionaries or emotion tags yet. What is AssemblyAI-TTS-1? AssemblyAI-TTS-1 is a streaming text-to-speech model from AssemblyAI that turns agent replies into speech for live calls. It was trained on millions of hours of audio, including real conversational data. Most TTS models represent audio as discrete tokens. AssemblyAI says TTS-1 operates on continuous audio representations instead. The AssemblyAI claims this improves realism and cuts time to first spoken audio. The launch includes a library of 4,000+ voices and instant voice cloning. A clone needs a short recording and a confirmation of the speaker’s permission. The clone in the launch post used 24 seconds of audio. Six languages are supported at launch: English, Spanish, French, German, Italian and Portuguese. How do developers integrate AssemblyAI-TTS-1? There are 3 interfaces: an HTTP API, a WebSocket API and an OpenAI-compatible route. The WebSocket session keeps one connection per conversation and accepts a cancel message for barge-in. Output is mono PCM, mu-law or A-law, at 8 kHz to 48 kHz. 24 kHz PCM is the native format; telephony stacks can request 8 kHz mu-law directly. Word timestamps are included. AssemblyAI also published LiveKit and Pipecat reference agents. How does AssemblyAI-TTS-1 perform on benchmarks? AssemblyAI tested TTS-1 against 5 models on 4 English sets, using 50 matched cloned voices. All figures below are self-reported, from an eval dated October 28, 2026. Entity accuracy (580 hard targets such as phone numbers and codes): 93.7%, vs ElevenLabs v4 93.6%, Cartesia Sonic 3.6 82.5%, ElevenLabs Flash v2.5 68.0%. Word accuracy: 99.0% on Seed-TTS and LibriSpeech sentences. Predicted MOS: 3.85, behind Inworld TTS-2 Flash at 3.88 and ahead of Sonic 3.6 at 3.82. Median time to first byte: 47 ms. Flash v2.5 took 119 ms, Sonic 3.6 143 ms, Inworld TTS-2 Flash 244 ms. Other: 85.5 TTSDS prosody score and 0.64 speaker similarity for cloned audio. Independent results are more mixed. On Cekura’s benchmark of 27 models, TTS-1 scored 81.5% reading accuracy and 4.50 naturalness. Its median streaming latency, timed from the last word sent, was 159 ms. Inworld TTS-2 Flash posted 45 ms and 93.2% accuracy there, at the same $15 price. AssemblyAI also cites a 1.7% word error rate on Coval’s leaderboard. It reports a top-10 debut in Artificial Analysis’ controlled-voice arena. Play

events.title: NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe: An Open 30B MoE Model for 40-Language Transcription with ~4B Active Parameters
events.summary:
NVIDIA released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, an open-weights speech LLM with 4.3B active parameters. It transcribes 40 languages, adds speaker labels and word timestamps, and posts a 4.71% mean WER on the English Open ASR Leaderboard.

The post NVIDIA Releases Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe: An Open 30B MoE Model for 40-Language Transcription with ~4B Active Parameters appeared first on MarkTechPost.
events.content:
NVIDIA has released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, an open-weights speech LLM built for transcription. One model handles 40 languages and recordings up to 1 hour. A text instruction picks the output style for each request. Options include verbatim, written form, speaker-attributed, contextual and translated output. For developers, it can replace separate ASR, diarization and alignment tools. TL;DR Size: 34B total and about 4.3B active parameters; 65,536-token context; audio up to 1 hour. Runs on: 1x H100 80 GB in BF16. FP8 (about 35 GB) and NVFP4 (about 21 GB) checkpoints exist; NVFP4 runs on an RTX 5090. GGUF files target NeMo-Speech.cpp. Performance: Best open-weights model on the English and multilingual Open ASR Leaderboards; top commercial APIs still lead. Best: 4.71% mean WER on the 9 public English Open ASR sets (next open model: 4.94%). Worst: 34.95% cpCER on AliMeeting Mandarin far-field meetings. Bottom line: Best thing: 1 open model covers transcripts, speaker labels, timestamps and translation. Worst thing: offline only, with weak Mandarin meeting accuracy. What is Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe? Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is a speech-augmented language model (SALM) from NVIDIA that turns audio and instructions into text. An audio encoder feeds embeddings into an LLM decoder, which makes transcription promptable. NVIDIA’s technical research report argues there is no single correct transcript. Numbers, fillers and domain terms depend on who reads the output. NVIDIA positions the model as a transcription specialist, not a general-purpose assistant. How does the architecture work? It has three parts: Parallel Expert Encoder: a trainable 0.6B Transformer ASR encoder runs beside a frozen Nemotron 3 Diarization model. The diarizer tracks up to 8 speakers. Its speaker activity is added to the ASR features every 80 ms. The LLM therefore sees who spoke when, without architecture changes. LLM backbone: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B, a hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE. It has 52 layers: 23 Mamba-2, 23 MoE and only 6 attention layers. Each MoE layer routes to 6 of 128 experts plus 1 shared expert. Few attention layers keep the KV cache small for hour-long audio. Add-ons: a shared multi-token prediction (MTP) layer drafts tokens for speculative decoding. A 50M-parameter CTC adapter aligns the finished transcript to audio for word timestamps. The model name says 30B-A4B, but the checkpoint holds about 34B parameters. The extra weight comes from the 1.3B MTP module and the audio components. Training used 1 supervised fine-tuning stage on 256 H100 GPUs for 28,500 steps. A short RL stage followed: 400 GSPO updates with a reward of 1 minus WER. The model saw about 1.72M unique hours of audio, or 6.5M hours with repeats. How does it score on benchmarks? All numbers below are self-reported by NVIDIA in the technical report. English Open ASR (9 public sets): 4.71% mean WER. The next open model, Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, scores 4.94%. Seven commercial systems still lead, topped by OtterAI speech-v3.1 at 3.88%. Multilingual Open ASR (7 languages): 4.62% mean WER, versus 6.49% for Qwen3-ASR-1.7B. ElevenLabs Scribe v2 reaches 3.56%. Long-form ASR: 10.98% mean WER, versus 13.37% for Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3. Multi-speaker, full sessions: 15.80% mean cpWER, versus 16.83% for DiCoW v3.3 with DiariZen. NVIDIA says it is the first SALM to beat cascaded systems here. Contextual ASR: an entity list cuts named-entity WER on ContextASR-Bench from 12.21% to 2.20%. Auto-play

events.title: Creating AI value with enterprise context
events.summary: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a…
events.content:
Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments.

DOWNLOAD THE REPORT

An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all.

Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes.

“There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.”

The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business. A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms). It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says.

Download the report

This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

events.title: Google DeepMind Introduces Gemini 4 Carbon, Its Top Model for Cyber Defense and Coding
events.summary:
Google DeepMind introduced Gemini 4 Carbon, a frontier model that scores 59 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro. Access starts with vetted cyber defenders, at $2/$10 per million tokens.

The post Google DeepMind Introduces Gemini 4 Carbon, Its Top Model for Cyber Defense and Coding appeared first on MarkTechPost.
events.content:
Google DeepMind has introduced Gemini 4 Carbon, its strongest model to date. Gemini 4 Carbon is a frontier model from Google built for long-horizon agentic coding and cybersecurity defense. It ranks #1 on the updated v5.0 Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 59. For developers, the catch is access. Carbon starts with a vetted group of cyber defenders, not the public API. TL;DR Size: Parameter count and context window not disclosed. Its predecessor, Gemini 4 Argon, has a 1,048,576-token context. Runs on: Google-hosted only. No open weights, no self-hosting, no quantized variants. Performance: Leads 15 of 17 published benchmarks versus Argon, GPT-6 Astra, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1. Best: 96.2% BFS F1 on GraphWalks (256K to 1M tokens), versus 84.2% for Argon. Worst: 81.5% on OSWorld-2.1, trailing Claude Opus 5.5 at 87.2%. Bottom line: Best: state-of-the-art vulnerability finding, exploitation and patching. Worst: you probably cannot call it yet. What is Gemini 4 Carbon? Carbon is the second Gemini 4 model, following Gemini 4 Argon. Google team states that the model targets hard, long-running engineering work. Internal teams saw Carbon run for days on single tasks. Examples include root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. Google also tuned Carbon for full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. On WebDev Arena, Carbon gained 89 Elo points to reach #4 at 1769. How does Gemini 4 Carbon perform on benchmarks? Google published a 17-row comparison in its launch post. Carbon was run at the highest thinking setting. Most rival numbers are self-reported by each provider, per Google’s evaluation methodology. Agentic coding: Carbon scores 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 (AA), ahead of Opus 5.5 at 59.6%. It hits 9.6% on SWE-sweep, narrowly ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 9.5%. On FrontierSWE, GPT-6 Astra leads at 65.5% versus Carbon’s 61.2%. Computer use and knowledge work: Carbon reaches 77.4% on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1. On Vending-Bench 2, it ends with a $16,484 bank balance, the highest listed. Long context and science: GraphWalks is the widest gap: 96.2% versus 71.8% for GPT-6 Astra. Carbon also posts 80.0% on RiemannBench. Why does Carbon relevant for cybersecurity? Google frames Carbon around the full defense lifecycle: find, validate, then fix. Cyber benchmarks were evaluated without guardrails. Finding: 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, versus 85.4% for GPT-6 Astra. Exploiting: 54.8% on ExploitGym, versus 42.4% for GPT-6 Astra and 34.5% for Opus 5.5. Patching: 71.0% on Collinear’s CWE-bench, versus 68.0% for Argon and GPT-6 Astra. Google computed SEC-bench Pro and ExploitGym scores itself, using its Antigravity harness. ExploitGym ran with mitigations off. Internally, Carbon showed more than 2x higher success at generating secure code than Argon. Google team states that the Chrome team found Carbon over 10x better than another lab’s model at high-quality patches. Wiz reports Carbon leading its web penetration testing benchmarks. Play the loop
1 · FindSEC-bench Pro: uncover real vulnerabilities
2 · ValidateExploitGym: check which flaws are exploitable
3 · PatchCWE-bench: fix the root cause in code

Cyber benchmarks evaluated without guardrails. Google self-computed SEC-bench Pro and ExploitGym (mitigations off). Not disclosed = no score published.

events.title: MiniMax Open-Sources MCode Stack: 15 Agent Skills Its Coding Team Uses Daily
events.summary:
MiniMax has open-sourced MCode Stack, an MIT-licensed repo of 17 SKILL.md skills and 5 checklists that its MiniMax Code team uses daily for code review, subagent splits, context budgets and long-running commands.

The post MiniMax Open-Sources MCode Stack: 15 Agent Skills Its Coding Team Uses Daily appeared first on MarkTechPost.
events.content:
MiniMax has open-sourced MCode Stack, the workflows and agent skills its team uses to build MiniMax Code. The MiniMax MCode Stack agent skills went public on October 28, 2026 under the MIT license. It is not a prompt collection. Each piece is a SKILL.md skill or checklist that installs directly into MiniMax Code. For developers, it turns harness engineering habits into steps an agent can actually run.

TL;DR

Size: 2 stacks, 17 skills (15 from Ronny, 2 from Jiachen), 5 checklists, 5 companion notes.

Runs on: Any machine running MiniMax Code (Node.js 22.19+) or Claude Code. No GPU. Skills are plain Markdown.

Performance: No benchmarks or eval results published.

Best: long-command-check, a 10-point audit for long shell commands and background tasks.

We just open-sourced MCode Stack: the actual workflows and skills the MiniMax Code team uses every day to build MiniMax Code. https://t.co/vREt7i8m2M
— RonnyHe (@Ronny_MiniMax) October 28, 2026 

What is MiniMax MCode Stack?

MCode Stack is an open-source repo of agent skills from MiniMax’s MiniMax Code team. MiniMax Code is the MiniMax’s open-source terminal coding agent, also MIT-licensed. The stack holds no MiniMax Code source code. It holds only workflows, skills and checklists.

The repo pairs with a column called MCode Engineering Notes. Each note explains one idea. The repo makes that idea runnable. Published notes cover subagents, tool context, compaction versus memory and long bash commands. A note on per-turn context tax is marked upcoming.

What skills are inside Ronny’s stack?

MiniMax’s stack ships 15 skills, grouped by moment in the working day:

Plan and split (3): subagent-split-check, engineering-small-prs, engineering-change-descriptions.

Context and tools (2): tool-budget-audit, context-tax-audit.

Long sessions and commands (3): long-session-check, handoff-doc, long-command-check.

Review (4): independent-review, engineering-code-review, engineering-review-comments, engineering-review-feedback.

Experiments and hotfixes (3): harness-experiment, trajectory-review, engineering-emergency-changes.

A few ideas stand out. independent-review gives the reviewer exactly 3 inputs: the diff, the requirement and test results. It deliberately withholds the author’s conversation. The reasoning: a reviewer inheriting the author’s context repeats the author’s blind spots.

subagent-split-check says to split work only when context is the measured problem. Splitting by team or question type is not a valid reason.

tool-budget-audit separates 2 costs: tool definitions and tool results. Tool search mainly cuts the first. Programmatic tool calling mainly cuts the second.

harness-experiment enforces 1 change per experiment. It tracks flipped tasks, requests per task, tokens, cache hit rate and wall-clock time.

The long-command checklist has 10 items. It asks whether moving a command to background re-runs the process. It also asks whether unread results survive compaction.

The 6 engineering-* skills are adapted from Google Engineering Practices. That material stays under CC-BY 3.0, per the stack’s NOTICE.

 

How do you install MCode Stack?

There are 3 paths, per the README:

One skill: clone the repo and copy a skill folder into ~/.agents/skills/.

Whole stack as a local plugin: copy stacks/ronny into MiniMax Code’s local plugin directory.

Marketplace: in MiniMax Code desktop, add the MiniMax-AI/mcode-stack marketplace. This option is rolling out gradually.

The same catalog works in Claude Code with /plugin marketplace add MiniMax-AI/mcode-stack. MiniMax Code also reads ~/.claude/skills/ and ~/.codex/skills/. The skills use the common SKILL.md format, so most work in other agents that support skills.

How does MCode Stack compare with other skill packs?

events.content:
GitHub Octoverse 2026

I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular:

This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month.

The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: 

Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location. Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...]

Industry. Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...]

Interoperability. Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation.

I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games.

 Tree Appreciator
 Emberwick
 Battle Drones
 Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove
 Four times as insulting
 What happens if someone actually puts the work in?
 You should build a game!

Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game:

3D modeling
Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox)
Game design (!)

That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments. The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play.

Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it.

Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did.

In the past few weeks I've vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term - no looking at the code at all) four games that I've genuinely enjoyed playing.

I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn't exist without AI assistance.

I haven't done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn't quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn't match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year.

Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser.

Tree Appreciator
The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator. I used the regular Claude chat interface for this - it didn't even need Claude Code.

I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was:

Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful.

I've found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn't have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent.

This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all - I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here. Here's the chat transcript that built it.

It's pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a "herbarium" provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment.

Emberwick
This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG:

Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening

events.content:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models

When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup, he didn’t think its data was worth much. But he’s since turned the company’s digital archives into tens of thousands of dollars, selling its codebase and workspace data.

He’s part of a growing market in which companies that help shut down startups sell their data to AI labs. Demand has grown as training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets, with buyers seeking real-world records to help train AI agents. But the sales raise legal and ethical questions.

Read the full story on the AI labs buying up the remains of failed startups.

—Matthew King

Are we there yet? Interspecies communication 

Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. 

Decoding how animals communicate with one another could reveal the inner lives of other species—and give humans a window onto how they see the world. A growing arsenal of devices and advances in AI have made it easier to study their howls, squeaks, and clicks, but making sense of it all remains complex.

Find out how close we are to interspecies communication.

—Cassandra Willyard

This story is part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue.

MIT Technology Review Narrated: what it would take to build a city on the moon

The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp.

A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining.

That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will.

events.title: Polymathic AI and Princeton Researchers Release FlashMap, a Flow Map Drafter for 6.14x Faster LLM Decoding
events.summary:
FlashMap is a speculative decoding drafter from Polymathic AI, Princeton and USC ISI researchers. It drafts 16 tokens jointly in one pass and reaches up to 6.14x lossless speedup on Qwen3-8B.

The post Polymathic AI and Princeton Researchers Release FlashMap, a Flow Map Drafter for 6.14x Faster LLM Decoding appeared first on MarkTechPost.
events.content:
Researchers from Polymathic AI, Princeton University, USC ISI, NYU and the Flatiron Institute have released FlashMap. FlashMap speculative decoding replaces the discrete diffusion drafter with a continuous flow map. It drafts a full 16-token block in 1 forward pass. Tokens in that block stay consistent with each other. On Qwen3-8B, the research team reports up to 6.14x lossless speedup on GSM8K. Drafter weights for Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B are on Hugging Face, with vLLM and SGLang plugins.

TL;DR

Size: 0.5B-parameter drafter (500M for Qwen3-8B, 475M for Qwen3-4B); drafts blocks of K = 16 tokens.

Runs on: the same GPU as the target model. Paper speedups use 1 NVIDIA H200 NVL at concurrency 1, in bf16.

Performance: fastest drafter tested on Qwen3-8B, about 7% above a retrained DFlash on average.

Best: 6.14x speedup on GSM8K at temperature 0 (acceptance length 7.69 tokens).

Worst: 2.28x speedup on Alpaca at temperature 1. On Qwen3-4B (temperature 0), it trails DFlash on 4 of 9 tasks.

What is FlashMap?

FlashMap is a speculative decoding drafter that maps Gaussian noise to a token block in 1 step. A small drafter proposes K tokens. The target model then checks all K in 1 parallel pass and keeps the longest matching prefix. Output stays exactly what the target would produce.

Speed depends on 2 things. How many drafted tokens get accepted, and how cheaply they were drafted. EAGLE-3 drafts autoregressively, so cost grows with block length. DFlash drafts the full block in 1 pass with block diffusion.

Why do diffusion drafters lose acceptance?

DFlash predicts each slot in the block independently. The research team calls this the factorized approximation. Picture a continuation that is “new york” or “san diego” with equal odds. An independent drafter proposes “new diego” or “san york” half the time. The target rejects those at slot 2.

FlashMap builds on Flow Map Language Models. Each noise sample maps to 1 full block. The noise picks the mode for every slot jointly.

How does FlashMap work?

The drafter is a 6-block diffusion transformer (DiT), with embedding dimension 2048 and 16 attention heads. It reads hidden states from target layers 1, 9, 17, 25 and 33. Embedding matrix and LM head are copied from the target and stay frozen.

Training runs in 2 stages:

Flow teacher: a continuous flow over one-hot token blocks, trained with cross-entropy. A time reparameterization handles Qwen3’s 151,936-token vocabulary.

Flow map student: semigroup distillation turns the flow into a 2-time denoiser. It jumps from noise to data in 1 step.

Both drafters train on 500K samples from Open-PerfectBlend. Total compute across all models and ablations was about 4,600 GPU hours on H200s.

 

How does FlashMap compare on benchmarks?

The research team retrained EAGLE-3 and DFlash on the same data and settings. Tests cover 9 benchmarks across math, code and chat, at temperatures 0 and 1.

Speed: 1-step FlashMap is the fastest drafter on every Qwen3-8B task, at both temperatures.

Accuracy: 1-step FlashMap beats DFlash on acceptance length in 15 of 18 settings. It has about half the parameters.

Chat gains are largest: at temperature 0, gains over DFlash are 5.5% on math, 11.1% on chat.

2-step mode: acceptance length beats DFlash in 18 of 18 settings, by 10% on average.

EAGLE-3: at temperature 1, it has 9% higher acceptance length but runs 35% slower.

A shuffle test checks whether drafts use real inter-token structure. At 2 steps, FlashMap recovers most of the joint-structure gain of a 16-step teacher. At 1 step, it keeps only a small fraction. Drafting 4 noise samples as a tree raised speedup by 11% on average.

events.title: Meet Google DeepMind’s Genie 4: Real-Time World Model With Native Audio
events.summary:
Google DeepMind released Genie 4 as a research preview. The real-time world model adds native audio, live dialogue and text steering, with Gemini 3.8 Flash planning events inside the simulation loop.

The post Meet Google DeepMind’s Genie 4: Real-Time World Model With Native Audio appeared first on MarkTechPost.
events.content:
Google DeepMind has released Genie 4 as a research preview for trusted testers. The Genie 4 world model generates explorable worlds from text and image prompts in real time. It also generates the soundscape: ambient noise, music and character dialogue. Users move with keyboard controls and steer events with plain-language prompts. The bigger change is architectural. A Gemini model now runs inside the simulation loop as a planner. That pattern is important for anyone building training environments for agents or robots.

TL;DR

Runs on: Google-hosted only (Project Genie web app, Gemini API early access). 

Performance: Photorealistic worlds with native audio and live text steering. 

Best: Scene consistency for up to 2 minutes, double Genie 3, per TechCrunch’s briefing.

Worst: Sessions last a few minutes, and objects drift after repeated prompt edits.

What is Genie 4?

Genie 4 is a world model from Google DeepMind that simulates interactive environments frame by frame. It is not a video clip generator. Each frame responds to user input as it arrives.

DeepMind states that the model is natively multimodal. Audio, music and dialogue are generated together with the visuals. It is DeepMind’s first real-time world model to generate audio natively.

It succeeds Genie 3, announced in August 2025. Genie 3 ran at 720p and 24 frames per second, with visual memory reaching back 1 minute.

How does Genie 4 use Gemini?

Genie 4 borrows from 2 parts of the Gemini family. Gemini Omni anchors the look and behavior of each world. Other Gemini models handle the reasoning that keeps a simulation coherent.

The runtime loop works like this:

Interpret: When you type a prompt, Gemini adapts it to fit the running scene.

Plan: Gemini 3.8 Flash breaks a goal into a sequence of steps.

Verify: It reviews incoming frames to confirm each step succeeded.

Adapt: If the world shifts or you intervene, it revises the plan.

Between user inputs, Gemini also steers the scene so the world keeps progressing. DeepMind team frames this as an early step toward hybrid world models. In that design, a language model handles structure and narrative, while Genie renders pixels and sound.

What can you do inside a Genie 4 world?

Steer with text: You can change the weather, move the camera or add a new person or object mid-session.

Simulate physics and people: DeepMind cites aerodynamics and collisions. It calls human motion the biggest leap, with characters that react to their surroundings.

Hear the world: Every world carries ambient audio. Characters can also hold conversations that react to your inputs in real time.

Test robot tasks: In one research demo, Gemini 4 Argon split a checkers task into steps. Genie 4 received each step as a text caption and simulated Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid playing the game.

How does Genie 4 compare with other world models?

events.title: Meet LEANN: An Open-Source Vector Index that Shrinks a 60M-Chunk RAG Index from 201 GB to 6 GB
events.summary:
UC Berkeley’s LEANN vector index stores a pruned graph and recomputes embeddings at query time. It matches HNSW accuracy at 90% recall using 4 GB instead of 188 GB, at the cost of seconds-level search.

The post Meet LEANN: An Open-Source Vector Index that Shrinks a 60M-Chunk RAG Index from 201 GB to 6 GB appeared first on MarkTechPost.
events.content:
UC Berkeley’s Sky Computing Lab built LEANN, an open-source vector index that stores almost no embeddings. The LEANN vector index recomputes embeddings at query time instead of saving them to disk. The repo benchmark shows a 60 million chunk Wikipedia index dropping from 201 GB to 6 GB. The research paper won the Best Research Paper award at MLSys 2026. So, it brings semantic search and RAG over personal data, on a laptop.

TL;DR

Size: 6 GB for 60M chunks (repo); 4 GB in the paper’s 76 GB Wikipedia setup. Default embedder: Contriever (110M params). It is an index, not an LLM, so no context length applies.

Runs on: laptops and workstations. The paper tested an RTX 4090 box with 32 GB RAM and an M1 Ultra Mac. A CPU-only Linux install exists, with no published CPU latency.

Performance: matches HNSW downstream accuracy at 90% recall, using under 5% of raw-data storage.

Best: 25.5% NQ accuracy, identical to HNSW, using 4 GB instead of 188 GB.

Worst: HotpotQA retrieval takes 44.80 s on the Mac, 50.1% of total pipeline time.

What is LEANN?

LEANN is a low-storage approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) index built on top of FAISS. It targets one problem: vector indexes are often bigger than the data they index. The research paper shows a 76 GB corpus needs 173 GB of embeddings plus a 15 GB HNSW graph. That more than doubles the raw data.

LEANN keeps a pruned graph, drops the full vectors, and rebuilds them on demand. The code is MIT licensed and installs with uv pip install leann. 

How does LEANN recompute embeddings without stalling search?

Graph indexes like HNSW visit only a small set of nodes per query. LEANN exploits that. It stores the graph plus a compact product quantization (PQ) table. At query time, it re-embeds only nodes on the search path.

3 techniques keep this practical:

Two-level search: cheap PQ distances rank neighbors first. Only top candidates get exact recomputation.

Dynamic batching: candidates from several hops are grouped, for example 64 at once, for GPU efficiency.

High-degree preserving pruning: most nodes keep few edges, while the top 2% “hub” nodes keep more.

In ablations, two-level search gives an average 1.4x speedup. Adding batching raises it to 1.8x. Embedding recomputation still accounts for about 76% of query latency.

 

How does LEANN perform on benchmarks?

The research team tested NQ, TriviaQA, GPQA and HotpotQA against a 60M-passage RPJ-Wiki datastore. Latency is measured at 90% Recall@3. All figures below are self-reported in the research paper.

On NQ, with Qwen3-4B on an RTX 4090, LEANN and HNSW both reach 25.5% downstream accuracy. LEANN uses 4 GB of storage. HNSW uses 188 GB. BM25 scores 18.3%, and PQ compression scores 17.9%.

The cost is search time. LEANN retrieval takes 2.48 s on NQ, versus 0.05 s for HNSW. Generation takes about 20 s, so end-to-end latency rises from 20.95 s to 23.34 s.

Across datasets on the RTX 4090, LEANN retrieval ranges from 1.12 s (GPQA) to 7.12 s (HotpotQA). The IVF-based recomputation baseline, inspired by EdgeRAG, is up to 200x slower. LEANN improves exact match by up to 11.8% over BM25.

The GitHub repo reports similar savings on personal data. 400K chat messages shrink from 1.8 GB to 64 MB. 38K browser entries shrink from 130 MB to 6.4 MB.

events.title: Liquid AI Releases LFM3: 6 Open-Weight 2B-Class Multimodal Models
events.summary:
Liquid AI released LFM3, 6 open-weight 2B-class models for text, vision, audio, omni and decisions. LFM3-1.7B uses a tri-hybrid backbone, a 256K context window and fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit.

The post Liquid AI Releases LFM3: 6 Open-Weight 2B-Class Multimodal Models appeared first on MarkTechPost.
events.content:
Liquid AI has released LFM3, its new generation of Liquid Foundation Models. Liquid AI LFM3 is a family of 6 open-weight, 2B-class models built on one shared backbone. The family covers text, vision, audio, omni and decision tasks. Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU. Developers can then deploy on phones, laptops, private servers or the cloud.

TL;DR

Size: LFM3-1.7B has 1.73B parameters and a 256K context window. LFM3-VL-2B has 1.92B and 128K. LFM3-Omni-2B has 2.2B.

Runs on: about 1 GB of memory at 4-bit, so phones and laptops. GGUF, MLX, ONNX, FP8 and NVFP4 checkpoints ship.

Performance: LFM3-1.7B averages 49.37 across 29 benchmarks, above Qwen3.5-9B at 47.24 (Liquid’s own eval).

Best: IFEval 96.66, and AutomationBench 41.29 vs 15.10 for Qwen3.5-9B.

Worst: Humanity’s Last Exam (no tools) 7.17, and RULER 128K 65.56 vs 87.11 for Qwen3.5-9B.

What is Liquid AI LFM3?

LFM3 is a multimodal model family from Liquid AI that branches 6 models from 1 base. All of them start from LFM3-1.7B-Base. 

The release includes:

LFM3-1.7B: a text model for local agents, post-trained for harnesses like Hermes Agent, Pi and OpenClaw.

LFM3-VL-2B: the first LFM vision model with video input, sampled at 2 fps.

LFM3-Audio-2B: speech in and out across 18 languages, with tool calling.

LFM3-Omni-2B: vision, audio and language in one model, answering in text or speech.

d1-2B and d1-Omni-2B: decision models that answer many questions in 1 forward pass.

How does the tri-hybrid architecture work?

The backbone mixes 3 operators across 24 layers. There are 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention layers and 6 global attention layers. The SWA window is 256 tokens. Convolution kernels grew from 3 to 7.

Liquid AI team found this mix with its hardware-in-the-loop architecture search. LFM2 was tuned on 1 phone and 1 laptop. LFM3 was tuned across 14 device and backend combinations. These include a Raspberry Pi 5 and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

Other changes include head-wise sigmoid gates on attention, partial RoPE on global layers and sandwich norm. The base model saw 22T tokens. The last 3.5T tokens were agent-heavy mid-training, which also extended context to 256K.

Post-training ran in 4 stages. SFT on 1.75T tokens came first, then mixed RL. Next, 6 specialist teachers were distilled into 1 model, followed by agentic RL.

How does LFM3-1.7B perform on benchmarks?

Liquid AI reports that LFM3-1.7B beats LFM2.5-2.6B with 35% fewer parameters. The bigger story is the agent results. On WebArena-Verified it scores 38.42, against 28.94 for Qwen3.5-9B. On BFCL V4 it scores 71.39, against 62.83.

Size still wins on knowledge and agentic coding. GPQA Diamond is 63.37, versus 80.40 for Qwen3.5-9B. SWE-bench Verified is 43.40, versus 51.20. Search narrows the gap: Humanity’s Last Exam rises from 7.17 to 13.90 with tools.

events.content:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Will the real Anthropic please stand up?

After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and how it believes it will change the world.

But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. Its public messaging is a master class in narrative capture, presenting it as different things to different people: an AI safety organization, a profit-driven megacorp, and a group hell-bent on creating superhuman technology.

These roles come with huge tensions. Will the IPO reveal the company behind the mask, or lean deeper into the myth-making? Take a new glimpse inside Anthropic.

—Will Douglas Heaven

This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.

How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom

Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping efficiently move power across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.

As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses.

The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid.

Find out how solid-state transformers could help meet rising electricity demand.

We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks, without the workout.

The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness.

Discover how close researchers are to developing an exercise pill.
